item.title: llama.cpp and AMD Launch Benchmark Dashboard for Local AI Inference
item.description:
llama.cpp and AMD Launch Benchmark Dashboard for Local AI Inference

The llama.cpp project and AMD have released a new benchmark dashboard for measuring local inference performance on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Available on Hugging Face, the dashboard enables developers to track prompt processing and text generation performance across different llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations.

📊 Overview

The dashboard is designed to make performance comparisons straightforward for AMD developers. Users can select specific hardware, models, and llama.cpp builds to compare quantizations and follow performance changes over time.

Key features include:

  • Tracking PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens)
  • Build history tab to monitor performance across all recorded builds
  • Context scaling tab to observe how token-generation throughput changes as context grows
  • Access to underlying benchmark results through public workflows

⚙️ Key Details

| Component | Description | |—|—| |————| | Hardware Options | Radeon 8060S (gfx1151), Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201) | | Test Metrics | PP512 and TG128, both starting at context depth zero | | Benchmark Frequency | Weekly public workflows | | Model Set | Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models | | GGUF Formats | Q4_K_M, Q8_0, BF16, F16 |

The benchmark workflows run with Flash Attention enabled and disabled, using 10 repetitions per configuration. Performance is measured as mean throughput (avg_ts) for both PP512 and TG128 tests.

🚀 Availability

The dashboard is hosted on Hugging Face and reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket. Users can click the data source link beside each chart title to access the underlying JSONL files for specific build, hardware, and model combinations.

Standard results follow the path format ///.jsonl, while workload sweeps use -tg.jsonl filenames.

💡 Why It Matters

This tool provides transparent, accessible performance data for local AI inference on AMD hardware, helping developers optimize their deployments and understand the impact of different quantization strategies and hardware configurations.

item.title: Music gear companies open-source devices in response to AI vibe-coding
item.description:
Music gear companies open-source devices in response to AI vibe-coding

The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools has created chaos in the music gear world, forcing companies to determine how to respond to a wave of AI-aided custom firmwares and modding communities. While some manufacturers have remained silent, others have decided to embrace the trend by opening up their devices and providing tools for the community.

🔍 Overview

As it became clear that no piece of music gear was safe from AI tools and curious tinkerers, companies began making their devices open source. Major names like inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, and Native Instruments, decided to “join ’em” rather than resist. Meanwhile, companies like Roland, Korg, Arturia, and Novation have yet to issue public statements on the matter.

⚙️ Key details

  • inMusic: inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell stated the company will provide a toolbox and the inner workings of devices like the MPC or Sample so people can do what they want. This includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key. Akai aims to walk a fine line by offering modders access while keeping products reliable for professionals, promising a “reset button” so users can experiment without losing their original setup.
  • Behringer: The company announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller. Launch dates for these products are currently unclear.
  • M-Vave: The company’s $70 pocketable clone of the Yamaha DX7 became popular due to its price and hackability, leading to more than a dozen custom firmwares. M-Vave responded by releasing an open-source firmware for developers and confirmed its successor, the FM-2, will also be open source.
  • Erica Synths: The company released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine. Founder Ģirts Ozoliņš noted the sustainability of using one device with various options instead of buying multiple “plastic boxes,” while acknowledging that vibe coding does not offset the environmental impact of data centers.
  • Polyend: Open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes and released the Endless guitar pedal last year, which allows users to vibe-code their own effects.
  • Elektron: The company banned links to custom firmware from its official forums, warning that modifications could brick machines, prevent updates, or affect warranty coverage. CPO Christian Alsing stated that while he is sympathetic to the hacker community and believes users have the right to modify their devices, he pushed back on accusations that the company is withholding features.

💡 Why it matters

The shift toward open-sourcing hardware and firmware reflects a strategic pivot in the music technology industry. Companies are balancing the potential for community innovation and sustainability against the risks of hardware instability and the environmental costs associated with AI development.

item.title: NVIDIA Releases cuDSS 1.0 and DuckDB Sirius Extension
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases cuDSS 1.0 and DuckDB Sirius Extension

NVIDIA has released version 1.0 of its cuDSS library for sparse linear systems and collaborated with DuckLabs to release Sirius, a GPU-accelerated extension for DuckDB, enabling high-performance analytical queries on NVIDIA hardware.

🧩 How cuDSS Works

The cuDSS library is designed to solve large sparse linear systems for engineering and scientific simulations. It targets numerically challenging sparse systems, particularly symmetric indefinite ones, by offering symmetry-preserving matching and scaling as well as Bunch-Kaufman pivoting.

  • Matching and Scaling: Uses the HSL MC64 algorithm from the HSL collection of Fortran codes. This feature preserves symmetry and is enabled by default in cuDSS 1.0, improving accuracy and reducing memory and performance penalties associated with previous nonsymmetric matching.
  • Bunch-Kaufman Pivoting: Allows 2×2 pivots to maintain factorization stability while preserving symmetry. The algorithm applies a local test to each column to choose between 1×1 pivots, interchanged 1×1 pivots, or 2×2 blocks.
  • Default Configuration: cuDSS 1.0 defaults to using matching and scaling with CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_MAX_DIAG_PRODUCT and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting with CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN. Users can restore previous behavior using CUDSS_CONFIG_FORCE_NONSYMMETRIC_MATCHING.

📊 cuDSS Performance

Benchmark matrices for cuDSS were selected from semiconductor design, manufacturing, and computer-aided engineering workflows, including circuit simulation, TCAD, thermal, structural, electromagnetic, and fluid dynamics. Performance was benchmarked against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0 using an NVIDIA B200 GPU and an Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPU.

Phase Geometric-Mean Speedup
Analysis 2.5x
Numerical Factorization 5.9x
Triangular Solve 151x

cuDSS performance has improved over previous releases, with optimizations for superpanels in factorization, multithreaded analysis, and tuned solve-phase kernels. Developers can access these gains by upgrading without changing application code.

🐝 Sirius for DuckDB

Sirius is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, released as a DuckDB core extension in partnership with DuckLabs.

  • Integration: Developers can install and load Sirius using two SQL commands (INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius;). It requires DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver.
  • Architecture: DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU using a CUDA backend.
  • Performance: In TPC-H benchmarks with data stored in Amazon S3, Sirius delivered significant speedups over CPU-based DuckDB.
    • At Scale Factor 1,000 (1 TB), total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds.
    • At Scale Factor 3,000 (3 TB), runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, a 4.69x speedup.
    • With tuned settings, a two-GPU AWS instance configuration achieved 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best CPU-based configurations, reducing query-time compute cost by up to approximately 79%.

🚀 Availability

The general availability of cuDSS marks it as a production-ready library for commercial applications. Sirius is available as a DuckDB core extension, with a download size of approximately 700 MB.

#NVIDIA #cuDSS #DuckDB #GPU #HighPerformanceComputing

Source: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers for Computational Engineering with NVIDIA cuDSS 1.0 | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Microsoft Fixes Bluetooth Audio Quality Issues in Windows 11
item.description:
Microsoft Fixes Bluetooth Audio Quality Issues in Windows 11

Microsoft has released preview builds for Windows 11 that resolve a long-standing audio quality problem affecting Bluetooth headphone users. The update ensures high-fidelity stereo audio continues even when the system switches between audio profiles during microphone usage.

🔍 Issue Overview

The problem occurred when Windows automatically switched from the A2DP stereo profile to the headset (hands-free) profile whenever an app or game activated the headset’s microphone. This switch caused significant audio quality drops due to bandwidth limitations in two-way mode.

🧩 Technical Solution

  • Bluetooth LE Audio devices now maintain full-range stereo fidelity while simultaneously using the device’s microphone
  • Users can select the new 2 channels, 16 bit, 48000Hz option from Settings > System > Sound > Output > {Bluetooth device} > Output settings > Format when microphone is active
  • The feature supports headphones, earbuds, and speakers that support 48kHz playback

⚙️ Key Details

Device Type Capability
Bluetooth LE Audio devices Full-range stereo fidelity with microphone active
Compatible devices Headphones, earbuds, speakers supporting 48kHz playback

🚀 Availability

The preview builds are available for Beta and Experimental channels. Windows 11 Insiders can access the fix by installing these preview builds released on Friday.

💡 Why It Matters

The improvement benefits users during game chat, voice calls, voice typing, and Copilot Chat voice functionality, ensuring consistent audio quality across all microphone-intensive applications.

#Windows #Bluetooth #Audio #Microsoft

Source: Microsoft testing fix for Windows 11 Bluetooth audio quality drops

item.title: LLM-Assisted Hardware Hacking Enables Custom Firmware and Interface Redesigns for Consumer Devices
item.description:
LLM-Assisted Hardware Hacking Enables Custom Firmware and Interface Redesigns for Consumer Devices

Large language models are being used to redesign and upgrade hardware devices through a process known as vibe hacking. By prompting tools like Claude Code or Codex, users are modifying various consumer electronics including televisions, digital cameras, synthesizers, and gaming consoles. This development has created a new market for custom software and led to a surge in developer-friendly gadgets.

🔍 Overview

  • Large language models (LLMs) can find hidden APIs and unpack firmware files located on websites.
  • Users can repackage hardware software to add new capabilities or redesign user interfaces.
  • This trend has empowered both professional developers and non-developers to build custom software for their own devices.
  • While many modifications target Android-based systems, hardware such as dishwashers and luxury cars often run similar underlying software that remains susceptible to these methods.

🧩 How it works

To modify hardware using an LLM, users typically follow a technical process involving specific permissions and debugging tools. For example, a developer in India named Gathin T used Claude Code to modify a Xiaomi Android TV by enabling USB debugging and applying permissions tweaks. Once established on the same Wi-Fi network, the chatbot can explore, unpack, and repackage firmware to the user’s liking.

⚙️ Key details

Device Category Example Hardware Modification Details
Televisions Android-based (Xiaomi) Redesigned interfaces, removed ads, and simplified input switching via CleanYourTV
Cameras Various Digital Cameras Added recording capabilities, higher resolutions, and new color profiles
Musical Gear M‑Vave FM‑1 Installed custom open-source firmware and new features on cheap synthesizers
Game Consoles PlayStation 5 Created scripts for cross-device controller use and enabled PlayStation 2 disc playback

🚀 Availability

The ability to hack hardware using LLMs saw a significant increase in late 2025 when Claude Code reached a functional milestone. Throughout 2026, the practice expanded as more people pointed these capabilities at their big screens and handheld devices. Notable repositories like CleanYourTV have appeared on GitHub, receiving thousands of pull requests and feature ideas from the community.

💡 Why it matters

This shift toward AI-assisted hardware modification is changing how manufacturers approach security and intellectual property. Luke Dicken, a gaming executive and former head of artificial intelligence at Take‑Two, predicted that the industry may respond with more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and a push toward streaming to prevent decompilation. Additionally, users who install vibe-coded firmware operate outside official support channels and may face technical issues that the manufacturer is not equipped to solve.

item.title: esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips
item.description:
esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips

esptool-js is a new Javascript implementation of esptool, a serial flasher utility for Espressif chips, that runs directly in supported web browsers using the Web Serial API.

🔍 Overview

The repository provides a tool for flashing firmware to ESP devices without requiring a local Python environment. It is designed to work with Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge version 89 or later, as well as Google Chrome on Android version 61 or later via the web-serial-polyfill compatibility layer.

🧩 How it works

The library operates through the following workflow:

  • Request access to a serial port using the Web Serial API, optionally filtering by USB vendor or product IDs.
  • Configure loader options and create an ESPLoader instance.
  • Connect to the ESP device and detect the chip, a process that resets the device.
  • Flash firmware images to the device.

Users can read firmware files from a File input or fetch request. Key configuration parameters include the starting address in flash, flash mode (e.g., “dio”), flash frequency (e.g., “40m”), and flash size (e.g., “4MB”). Users can also set options to erase the entire flash before writing, compress data during transfer, or reset the device after flashing.

⚙️ Key details

Unlike the Python-based esptool, esptool-js does not implement generation of binary images out of ELF files and does not include companion tools similar to espefuse.py and espsecure.py.

Handling Flash Images

  • Merged .bin files: These are contiguous images where bytes between partitions are 0xFF. Using writeFlash erases every sector from the start of the image through its end, which also erases NVS and factory partitions within that span.
  • Sparse Intel HEX files: These leave gaps out. The parseIntelHex function splits the file into one { data, address } entry per contiguous region. If two regions share a 4 KiB flash sector, parseIntelHex throws an error. To ensure only covered sectors are erased, users should keep eraseAll: false and compress: true.

🚀 Availability

Developers can integrate esptool-js into web applications using the following endpoints:

  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/bundle.js for a single-file browser load. Dependencies such as pako are inlined, so no import map is required.
  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/lib/index.js for Node and bundlers. An API documentation reference is available for detailed class and method information.

#Espressif #WebAssembly #JavaScript #IoT #EmbeddedSystems

item.title: Sam Altman clarifies remarks on memory and local AI
item.description:
Sam Altman clarifies remarks on memory and local AI

Sam Altman has addressed the context of his previous comments regarding personal computer memory and data centers, clarifying that his remarks about centralizing memory usage were misinterpreted.

📢 New Clarifications

Speaking onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday, Altman stated that he wants people to have a lot of RAM and that everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer. He also noted that “home tinkering is great.”

These comments follow his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he said it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. Altman previously stated on X that the original remarks had been “taken out of context” and reiterated his desire for users to have “so much ram.”

🔍 The Context

  • Memory Usage: Altman suggested that “share this memory” and explained that if the world is in a memory supply shortage, it might be optimal to have memory working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device.
  • Misinterpretation: Altman stated, “That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by,” explaining that he was trying to discuss the optimal use of limited supply, though he noted that people having their own at-home inference is a tradeoff.
  • Supply Chain Issues: Altman commented that OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” including memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
  • Supply Shortage: He noted that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular,” but “the world did not build out that much,” resulting in DRAM prices potentially going up “5x, 7x, something like that.”
  • Jensen Huang: Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

💡 Why It Matters

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman’s clarifications highlight the tension between the need for centralized data center memory and the value of personal computer hardware for local inference.

#OpenAI #AI #SAM-Altman #Memory-Shortage #Data-Centers #Tech

Source: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’

item.title: Detecting Silent Data Corruption in Distributed Model Training on SageMaker HyperPod
item.description:
Detecting Silent Data Corruption in Distributed Model Training on SageMaker HyperPod

Silent data corruption (SDC) occurs when a GPU returns a wrong but plausible number without raising an error. In large‑scale distributed training the erroneous value can propagate through gradients and weights of every replica, keeping loss seemingly normal for hours before a divergence is noticed.

🔍 Overview

  • SDC is caused by manufacturing defects or silicon aging, often in a multiply‑accumulate lane of a tensor core.
  • The compute path has no ECC or parity; a result like 4.0001 instead of 4.0000 passes unnoticed.
  • Existing safeguards (ECC memory, Xid errors, DCGM health checks, transport checksums, checkpoint checksums) do not catch SDC because they monitor different boundaries.
  • Meta observed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions during a 54‑day Llama 3 405B pre‑training run on up to 16 K H100 GPUs and traced them to SDC.

🛠️ Detection Method

Three lightweight checks are added to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop. When a check fires, the suspect rank is mapped to its Kubernetes node, the job is paused, and SageMaker HyperPod replaces the faulty node.

Check What it Detects When it Runs
Non‑finite gradient check NaN, Inf, or overflow in a GPU’s forward/backward pass and NaN/Inf introduced by all‑reduce Every training step before the all‑reduce
Ring replay audit Finite but wrong values by recomputing another node’s micro‑batch and comparing loss bits and gradient fingerprints Periodic audit steps
Weight fingerprint comparison Corruption in the optimizer step or stored weights by comparing each replica’s weights after the update After each optimizer update

📊 Validation

  • Tests were run on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs).
  • Software‑injected faults were introduced and each test was repeated on three instances, the minimum required for the checks.
  • The full implementation is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.

⚙️ Integration with SageMaker HyperPod

  • HyperPod’s health‑monitoring agent replaces nodes that report a fault (GPU errors, deep health‑check failures).
  • SDC slips past these mechanisms because the hardware never reports an error.
  • The detection workflow leverages the Kubernetes node name (which contains the instance ID) to map a suspect rank to a physical node, cordon the node, examine GPU metrics on the HyperPod observability dashboards, and then replace the node before resuming from a checkpoint saved prior to the suspect window.

💡 Why it matters

  • Early detection prevents wasted compute on hours of silently corrupted training.
  • Containing the fault at the node level avoids larger job interruptions.
  • The approach adds minimal overhead and works with existing SageMaker HyperPod infrastructure.

#SilentDataCorruption #DistributedTraining #SageMaker #GPU

Source: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Internal Investigation Into Extramarital Affairs
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Internal Investigation Into Extramarital Affairs

Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO, president, and board member of Nvidia, the company he co-founded in 1993. The resignation follows a board investigation into two reported extramarital affairs, including one with a direct report and another with an alleged surveillance operative. CFO Colette Kress has been appointed as interim CEO while the board conducts a search for a permanent successor.

🔍 Overview

Following a board meeting on Wednesday night, the company accepted Huang’s resignation effective immediately. This leadership change introduces a new corporate structure and temporary management team:

  • Interim CEO: Colette Kress, who has served as Nvidia’s CFO for over 13 years.
  • Board Chair: Harvey Jones has been appointed as the first-ever Chair of the Board in NVIDIA’s history.
  • Succession Plan: The board is initiating a search for a permanent CEO, evaluating both internal and external candidates.

⚙️ Key details

The board’s investigation focused on two specific relationships involving Huang. One relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s VP of healthcare, who reported directly to the CEO. The second involved Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

According to reports, Alice Huang was allegedly a surveillance operative passing information regarding advanced AI chips to China’s Ministry of State Security. While Huang admitted to being unfaithful and apologized to his family and employees, concerns have been raised regarding whether these relationships influenced business decisions or government export controls.

📊 Potential Successor Candidates

Reports have identified several high-profile individuals as potential candidates for the permanent CEO role:

Candidate Current Role / Organization
Colette Kress Interim CEO and CFO, Nvidia
Johny Srouji Hardware Chief, Apple
Ian Buck Vice President, Nvidia
Lisa Su CEO, AMD
Rene Haas CEO, Arm

💡 Why it matters

Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world, serving as the primary provider of chips fueling AI advancement. The company maintains an investment portfolio worth approximately $99 billion and holds significant influence over the global economy. Under Huang’s 33-year leadership, Nvidia defined the modern GPU and pioneered the platform that powers the current AI revolution. The company will host a meeting for employees to discuss the transition on November 18 at 9am PT.

item.title: Anthropic details multi‑chip strategy and compute multipliers in IPO roadshow
item.description:
Anthropic details multi‑chip strategy and compute multipliers in IPO roadshow

Anthropic kicked off its IPO roadshow yesterday, releasing a video that reveals new details about how the company trains and serves its Claude models.

🔍 Overview

  • Anthropic trains and serves Claude across four major chip families: AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
  • The company attributes this capability to an early, unconventional bet on a multi‑chip strategy, despite initial skepticism that the effort was not worthwhile.

🧩 How it works

  • Each chip family requires its own tailored software and inference stack, which is traditionally expensive and difficult to build.
  • Anthropic says it has been doing this for years and has become “incredibly good” at it.
  • This year the team began working with AMD GPUs for the first time. Previously, adding a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work.
  • Using their internal tool Mythos, Claude was running on AMD GPUs in just three days with essentially no human intervention, and Claude itself ported or wrote almost 100% of the required kernels.

⚙️ Compute multipliers

  • Anthropic focuses on total effective compute, defined as physical capacity multiplied by discovered compute multipliers.
  • A discovered multiplier increases the effective compute pool; for example, a 4× multiplier lets the same model be trained with only a quarter of the physical compute, or lets the same physical compute train a more capable model.
  • Multipliers are cumulative: each new multiplier positively impacts the ones discovered earlier, and they “stack.”
  • The company believes this effect will accelerate as it approaches recursive self‑improvement, eventually allowing Claude to discover compute multipliers autonomously, causing the number of multipliers to grow faster and faster.

📈 Competitive advantage

  • The combination of a mature multi‑chip strategy and a rapid rate of compute‑multiplier discovery creates a competitive advantage that is hard for others to replicate.
  • Anthropic previously hinted at its multi‑chip approach in a September post‑mortem describing TPU‑specific bugs, showing the long‑term focus on cross‑hardware robustness.

item.title: NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning
item.description:
NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning

AI workloads are moving beyond the data center. Developers are building agents that run at the edge—monitoring driver attention, helping robots navigate, and coordinating production‑line fleets. These applications must operate within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. NVIDIA now offers the DGX Spark platform in a 64 GB configuration together with the TensorRT Edge‑LLM runtime, enabling developers to prototype, fine‑tune, and test large‑language models such as Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning directly on edge hardware.

🔍 Overview

  • Physical AI agents need compact, low‑latency inference.
  • DGX Spark 64 GB provides the compute and memory headroom for edge prototyping.
  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM delivers a lightweight C++ inference runtime for embedded targets (Jetson Thor, DRIVE AGX Thor, IGX Thor).

🧩 How it works

  • The trtedge command‑line interface (CLI) downloads the selected model (≈21 GB) and builds TensorRT engines optimized for the Spark platform.
  • Once built, engines are cached in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm and reused on later launches.
  • A local OpenAI‑compatible API server can host the model, confirming readiness with a "status":"ready" JSON response.
  • DSpark speculative decoding can be enabled: a draft model proposes several tokens, which the main model validates in a single pass, reducing generation latency.

⚙️ Key details

  • Required software stack: NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer (10.x series), Python 3.10‑3.12.
  • Tested versions: TensorRT Edge‑LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.
  • Use a Python virtual environment to keep newly installed packages separate while still accessing system‑wide TensorRT libraries.
  • Verify the TensorRT version with the provided check command; if bindings are missing, install the compatible TensorRT 10.x package via the NVIDIA TensorRT pip instructions.
  • First launch downloads the model and builds the engine; subsequent launches reuse cached engines, accelerating startup.

🚀 Performance

  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM with Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning yields low response latency and fast token generation on DGX Spark 64 GB.
  • DSpark speculative decoding (using three draft tokens) improves generation speed; the exact time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT) and token‑per‑second rates are reported in the reference table.
  • Users can tune num_speculative_tokens and other settings to balance speed and accuracy for their workload.

📦 Availability

  • The tutorial demonstrates running the text‑only Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning model on Spark and enabling DSpark speculative decoding.

item.title: OpenAI’s RAM Buying Spree Tightens Global Memory Supply
item.description:
OpenAI’s RAM Buying Spree Tightens Global Memory Supply

OpenAI’s rapid acquisition of DRAM has drawn attention to a growing shortage of RAM worldwide. CEO Sam Altman warned that keeping large amounts of memory in personal computers is “terrible” when the same chips could be better utilized in data‑center clouds.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI is buying massive quantities of DRAM for its cloud‑based AI workloads. The company’s purchasing power has led to long‑term contracts with the biggest memory manufacturers, effectively reserving a large share of the world’s RAM output for the next few years.

📦 Supply Chain Impact

  • OpenAI’s buying spree is squeezing the world’s supply of RAM.
  • Samsung and SK Hynix have signed long‑term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate, reserving much of the upcoming RAM production.
  • The billions of dollars spent on chips are a factor behind rising prices for laptops, phones, and other consumer devices.

🖥️ Why Data‑Center RAM Matters

“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open‑source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply‑constrained environment.”

Altman argues that keeping DRAM idle in personal machines wastes scarce resources; cloud‑scale deployment yields far higher utilization.

💰 Economic Ripple

  • The high demand for RAM by AI developers translates into higher hardware costs for everyday consumers.
  • As memory manufacturers allocate more production to cloud operators, smaller‑scale buyers face tighter inventories and price pressure.

The situation highlights a broader tension between the push for local AI inference and the physical limits of global memory supply.

item.title: NVIDIA Adds Eight‑Node DGX Spark Support, Enabling 1 TB Unified Memory for Frontier Models
item.description:
NVIDIA Adds Eight‑Node DGX Spark Support, Enabling 1 TB Unified Memory for Frontier Models

AI developers aren’t just running a single model anymore—they’re orchestrating multiple models in parallel, chaining inference calls, and experimenting with frontier‑class architectures that demand hundreds of gigabytes of memory.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA announced at GTC Berlin official support for eight‑node DGX Spark clusters. The new configuration scales unified memory to 1 TB, opening the door to frontier‑class models, multi‑agent workloads, and near‑linear pre‑training, all on‑premises.

🧩 How it works

  • Memory scaling: a single DGX Spark node provides 128 GB unified memory; four nodes give 512 GB; eight nodes reach 1 TB.
  • Model support: the 1 TB pool can host models that previously wouldn’t start on a four‑node system, exemplified by the full GLM 5.3 (753B) model from Z.ai.
  • Interactive serving: the eight‑node cluster can run the GLM 5.3 Flash checkpoint and deliver roughly 80 tokens per second (TPS) in generation, suitable for interactive local development.
  • Cluster management: NVIDIA Sync provides easy clustering; its Cluster Assistant handles setup and device management. Support for eight‑node clusters in NVIDIA Sync is slated for the end of the year.

⚙️ Key details

  • Collective communication: Tensor‑parallel inference spends a meaningful fraction of time in collective operations such as all‑reduce.
  • RoCEnante backend: a Spark‑optimized collective backend that reduces latency for small‑message, low‑concurrency, modest‑rank‑count patterns typical of tensor‑parallel decode on local AI hardware.
    • Implements an all‑to‑all exchange followed by local reduction using a single GPU kernel.
    • Fewer communication steps than ring all‑reduce; each rank shares its full input with every peer.
    • Benefits: lower latency for small messages and modest rank counts.
    • Trade‑off: increased data movement; less efficient as messages or rank count grow.
  • When to use NCCL: for high concurrency, larger clusters, or ring topologies, NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) performs better.
  • Performance gains (non‑quantized model):
    • ~5 % higher prefill throughput and ~21 % higher decode throughput at four nodes (NVFP4).
    • ~18 % higher decode throughput at eight nodes.
  • Integration: the RoCEnante backend is merged into FlashInfer and falls back transparently to NCCL if its startup test fails. It applies only to switch‑connected topologies.
Backend Best for Trade‑off
RoCEnante Small messages, low concurrency, modest rank count (e.g., 4–8 nodes) More data movement; latency advantage diminishes as rank count grows
NCCL High concurrency, larger clusters, ring topologies Slightly higher latency for small‑message patterns

🚀 Availability

  • Official eight‑node DGX Spark cluster support announced at GTC Berlin.
  • NVIDIA Sync will include eight‑node clustering capabilities by the end of the year.
  • RoCEnante backend is already integrated into FlashInfer for switch‑connected clusters.

💡 Why it matters

  • The unified 1 TB memory pool lets developers run frontier‑class mixture‑of‑experts models locally, reducing reliance on remote cloud resources.
  • Interactive token‑generation speeds (≈80 TPS) make on‑premise experimentation with large models feasible.
  • Optimized collective communication (RoCEnante) improves decoding throughput, directly benefiting generation latency for multi‑GPU deployments.

item.title: NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell
item.description:
NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell

NVIDIA announced Sentry, a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Sentry is part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture unveiled at GTC Berlin and runs on NVIDIA BlueField‑4 DPUs.

🔍 Overview

  • Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and stays within defined operational boundaries.
  • It provides host‑isolated runtime protection, controlling the agent’s only path to the model and offering tamper‑evident traceability of agent activity.
  • The framework works even when host resources cannot be trusted, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain.

🧩 How it works

  • Built on NVIDIA DOCA and deployed on BlueField‑4 DPUs, Sentry sits on the node’s sole path to the model and to the outside world.
  • Agent‑to‑model communications are inspected out‑of‑band; Sentry does not rely on the agent to report its own behavior.
  • Real‑time situational awareness is achieved through out‑of‑band observability, continuously evaluating runtime security and behavior.
  • Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment (e.g., container or microVM) to detect external threats and misbehavior.

⚙️ Key components

Component Role
BlueField‑4 DPU Executes Sentry in an isolated trust domain, intercepting all agent traffic before it reaches the host or model.
DOCA Flow Implements a layer‑4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon, blocking unauthorized destinations.
DOCA Tower Transparent proxy built on Envoy; performs layer‑7 inspection, authorization, and TLS termination with in‑silicon acceleration.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) Evaluates access requests against defined policies using the Rego language; runs locally in memory with sub‑millisecond latency.
DOCA Argus Provides live memory introspection of the host, mapping containers, microVMs, processes, threads, and resource relationships to give Sentry contextual evidence.

📡 Network protection

  • Layer‑4 firewall (DOCA Flow) blocks connections to unauthorized destinations.
  • Permitted traffic is forwarded to DOCA Tower for layer‑7 inspection and additional security checks.
  • DOCA Tower terminates TLS using built‑in silicon acceleration, ensuring encrypted traffic is inspected safely.
  • All network traffic reaches BlueField‑4 via a direct I/O path that bypasses host OS and hypervisor packet processing.
  • Policy evaluation is performed by OPA, which can decide on requests in under a millisecond.

📈 Runtime monitoring

  • Out‑of‑band observability continuously evaluates agent behavior for security and integrity.
  • Memory introspection supplies context about containers, microVMs, and other execution environments.
  • DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing volatile host memory on BlueField‑4 and remaining beyond the reach of compromised host software.

Nouveau/NVK Driver Runs on NVIDIA Spark Box After Extensive Patching

After much back and forth and hoops jumping, I can finally reveal nouveau/nvk running on a NVIDIA Spark box.

🔍 Overview

  • The open‑source nouveau/nvk driver has been demonstrated on a NVIDIA Spark platform.
  • The effort involved a large patch series and new firmware.

🛠️ What was required

  • 100 patches were prepared for the driver.

🚀 Availability

  • Upstreaming is still uncertain; the author is “not sure how best to upstream it all.”

📺 Watching the demo

  • To view the live stream of the demonstration, go to the YouTube schedule overview and hover over the paperclip to see the ‘Live Stream’ link.
  • Live streams are only available for A/V assisted tracks.
  • For a two‑way conversation during the stream, you need a Matrix account, join the Linux Plumbers Space, and find the room corresponding to the track you’re watching.

⚠️ ACPI Operation Region Conflicts (Related Kernel Insight)

  • Many people mistakenly think warnings like ACPI Warning: SystemIO range … conflicts with OpRegion … indicate a firmware bug; this is generally untrue.
  • The Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) specification abstracts hardware details.
  • ACPI provides information as code via the ACPI Source Language (ASL), which is compiled into bytecode interpreted by the OS at runtime.
  • ASL can define Operation Regions that map to hardware registers.
  • Example: an operation region OPR1 at I/O port 0x400, 2 bytes long, with 8‑bit fields INDX and DATA.
  • ACPI methods lock access to these registers; however, a Linux driver that accesses the hardware directly has no knowledge of ACPI and can race with ACPI methods.
  • The kernel detects such conflicts and emits warnings such as: ACPI Warning: SystemIO range 0x0000000000000400-0x000000000000401 conflicts with OpRegion 0x0000000000000400-0x0000000000000401 (OPR1).
  • This warning indicates a driver is attempting to allocate I/O ports that an ACPI operation region already claims.

All statements are drawn directly from the provided evidence.

item.title: NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput
item.description:
NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput

NVIDIA demonstrated that running a 32K‑input/1K‑output LLM inference workload inside confidential virtual machines (CVMs) on a Blackwell‑based DGX B200 system keeps almost all of the baseline performance.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) provides memory‑encrypted CVMs, confidential GPUs, and encrypted NVLink, enabling LLM inference to run securely while preserving throughput.

🧩 How it works

  • Secure data path – The Blackwell CC architecture enforces hardware‑based protection for data and workloads in use.
  • Host‑to‑device transfer – In the B200 CC, transfers go through a software‑encrypted bounce buffer because the GPU cannot directly access protected CVM memory.
  • TensorRT LLM adaptations
    • Uses CC‑aware memory selection, opting for pageable memory on protected paths instead of always using pinned memory.
    • Moves repeated‑token and sampling‑data readback to an asynchronous worker, so protected copies do not block the main scheduler during decode.
    • Measures tactics with the GPU %globaltimer inside CC while keeping CUDA events outside CC.
  • NVLink limitation – NVLS (NVLink SHARP) multicast is not available in B200 CC configurations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model: nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4
  • Inference framework: TensorRT LLM (Docker container) with PyTorch backend
  • Sequence lengths: 32K input, 1K output
  • Parallelism: TP=8, EP=1, PP=1; KV cache in FP8
  • Concurrency tested: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 requests
  • Hardware: 1 NVIDIA DGX B200 system (8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs), GPU power limit 1,000 W
  • Platform: Intel TDX
  • Host OS / kernel: Ubuntu 25.10 / 6.17.0-20-generic
  • Guest OS / kernel: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS / 6.8.0-124-generic, 256 vCPUs, 2 NUMA nodes
  • Driver / software stack: NVIDIA driver 595.71.05, VBIOS FW 1.4.x, CUDA 13.2, TensorRT LLM 1.3.0rc22, NCCL v2.30, OpenSSL 3.6.0, Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit

📈 Performance results

  • Across concurrency levels 1–16, CC retained 96.1 %–98.2 % of the output‑token throughput compared with a non‑confidential baseline.
  • Mean TPOT (time‑per‑output‑token) stayed within 1.2 %–4.3 % of the baseline.
  • These results show that the security overhead of CC is limited to a few percent while providing full data protection.

💡 Why it matters

The Blackwell confidential computing architecture creates a hardware‑enforced security path that protects data in use without sacrificing most of the inference performance required for large‑scale LLM deployments.

Source: Enabling Private High-Performance Production AI Inference with NVIDIA Confidential Computing | NVIDIA Technical Blog

Powered by the S11 chip, the Series 12 introduces a Health Sensing System combining electrical and optical sensors to measure heart rate variability (HRV) and heart rate every five seconds.

  • AI Integration: watchOS 27 brings Siri AI to the device to combine personal context with broader knowledge. New Audio Intelligence capabilities will arrive later this year.
